footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: I debated in a dream regarding the case in Yevamot 37a:

paragraphs.text: Yevamot 37a: ‘§ The mishna states that if a yevama consummated the levirate marriage and gave birth seven months later, there is an uncertainty whether the child is nine months old, counting from conception, and is the offspring of the first husband, i.e., the deceased brother, or whether the child is only seven months old and is the offspring of the second husband. If it is the child of the first husband, then there was never any obligation of levirate marriage, and the supposed consummation was in fact forbidden by penalty of karet. Due to that possibility, both the man and the woman are obligated to bring a guilt-offering for uncertainty. Rava said to Rav Naḥman: How can they bring a guilt-offering…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Yevamot 37a) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“I debated in a dream regarding the case in Yevamot 37a: where a child's paternity is doubtful between nine months to the first husband or seven months to the levir, such that one child is legitimate while the other...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Yisrael Kedoshim 4:2 (§10): “Even though one is already bound by the oath of Mount Sinai; because the yetzer deceives him into thinking it is permissible, wherefore a personal oath is effective; and similarly in that incident he imagined she was permitted as a concubine (pilegesh), wherefore the fence of Ezra's immersion assisted him! The theme: The Torah residing within the heart versus external knowledge, Doeg’s hypocrisy, and the engraving upon the heart. Scholars might assume that through their Torah the yetzer is confused and powerless, for Midrash Tehillim (119:11) states on "Your word have I laid up in my heart": whoever possesses Torah in his heart, the yetzer hara has no dominion over him.” Connection to this note: In Yisrael Kedoshim 4:2 (§10), Rav Tzadok develops this theme alongside Yevamot 37a, illuminating how the teaching in Divrei Chalomot 21 unfolds within Kisvei Rav Tzadok.

paragraphs.text: Bava Batra 58a: ‘§ The Gemara relates additional incidents involving Rabbi Bena’a: There was a certain individual who said to his family before he died: A barrel of earth to one of my sons, a barrel of bones to one of my sons, and a barrel of wads of wool to one of my sons. They did not know what he was saying to them. They came before Rabbi Bena’a for guidance. Rabbi Bena’a said to them: Do you have land that your father left as an inheritance? They said to him: Yes. He asked: Do you have livestock that your father left as an inheritance? They said: Yes. He asked: Do you have quilts [bistarkei] that your father left as an inheritance? They said: Yes. He said to them: If so, this is what he said to you,…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Bava Batra 58a) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“Yet one must consider Rabbi Bena'ah in Bava Batra 58a who relied on behavioral assessment to identify brazen sons as illegitimate for inheritance, though in monetary matters we do not follow a presumption to extract...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Ketubot 85b: ‘The Gemara examines cases involving disputes concerning the property of the deceased. There was a certain man who deposited seven pearls [marganita] tied up in a sheet in the house of Rabbi Meyasha, son of the son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Rabbi Meyasha passed away without instructing the members of his household on his deathbed, and without explaining to whom the gems belonged. Rabbi Meyasha’s family and the depositor came before Rabbi Ami to discuss the ownership of the gems. He said to them: They belong to the claimant, first of all, since I know about Rabbi Meyasha, son of the son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that he is not wealthy enough to be able to afford such gems. And…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 21, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Ketubot 85b) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“resembling Ketubot 85b ("my estate to Tuvia") where the court exercises judicial discretion (shuda dedayane) according to Rashi to assess the testator's intent; and subsequently I saw the Rashbam in Bava Batra...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Machshavot Charutz 17:14 (§7): “And regarding what the Sages stated: that the ministering angels argued, "Who will bring offerings before You, etc."; it appears to me that the ministering angels allegorically denote the Rabbis, as written in Nedarim (20b); and so was the matter reflected in the earthly kingdom: when Ahasuerus consulted the Sanhedrin, they recused themselves from the judgment of Vashti; not wanting the verdict to issue through their judicial decree; not considering themselves worthy that the miracle be wrought through their agency.” Connection to this note: In Machshavot Charutz 17:14 (§7), Rav Tzadok develops this theme alongside Ketubot 85b, illuminating how the teaching in Divrei Chalomot 21 unfolds within Kisvei Rav Tzadok.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Tzidkat HaTzadik 262 (§13): “And this is the "counterbalance repentance" (teshuvat hamishkal) instituted by the early masters, as is known, for regarding the outward garments of thought, speech, and action, remorse alone suffices, stripping off filthy garments and donning festive robes of Torah and mitzvot. paragraphs.text: Yevamot 71b: ‘Rabba bar Yitzḥak said that Rav said: The mitzva of uncovering the corona during circumcision was not given to our Patriarch Abraham. The command given to Avraham included only the mitzva of circumcision itself, i.e., the removal of the foreskin, but not the uncovering of the corona, i.e., the folding back of the thin membrane that lies under the foreskin. As it is stated: “At that time the Lord said to Joshua: Make yourself knives of flint, and circumcise again the children of Israel a second time” (Joshua 5:2). Why was it necessary to circumcise them? Apparently, it is because before the Torah was given on Mount Sinai, some of them had been circumcised in the manner of Abraham, without…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 22, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Yevamot 71b) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“though he circumcised Israel a second time through the uncovering (pri'ah) granted to Joshua (Yevamot 71b; Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 29), revealing the holy Yesod of Israel; and previously at the Exodus our Sages taught...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 3a: ‘The Gemara comments: And it stands to reason like the one who says that Rabbi Yishmael was speaking of a spirit of purity, as it is taught in a baraita: “And he warned his wife,” i.e., the issuing of the warning, is optional, that the husband is neither enjoined to nor prohibited from issuing a warning; this is the statement of Rabbi Yishmael. Rabbi Akiva says: It is mandatory, as one who sees his wife behaving in an inappropriate manner with another man is obligated to warn her. The Gemara explains: Granted, if you say that Rabbi Yishmael was speaking of a spirit of purity, then it is well, as it may be optional, or even mandatory, to issue a warning. But if you say that he was speaking…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 22, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Sotah 3a) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“for corruption of Yesod occurs solely through folly, as stated (Sotah 3a): "A person does not commit a sin unless a spirit of folly enters him"; and so with the tongue: "he who utters slander is a fool" [Proverbs...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

Rashi: the “harlot’s forehead” is brazenness — the unblushing face of one who refuses to be shamed. paragraphs.text: Eruvin 18b: ‘The Sages taught: With regard to one who counts out money for a woman from his hand into her hand or from her hand into his hand, in order to look upon her, even if in other matters he is like Moses our teacher, who received the Torah from Mount Sinai, he will not be absolved from the punishment of Gehenna. The verse says about him: “Hand to hand, the evil man shall not go unpunished” (Proverbs 11:21). One who hands money from his hand to her hand, even if he received the Torah from God’s hand to his own, like Moses, he will not be absolved from the punishment of Gehenna, which is called evil.’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 22, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Eruvin 18b) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“these being the "Jewish demons" in the Zohar generated from involuntary emissions of great men (Eruvin 18b regarding Adam); which explains why Joshua burned Hazor alone (Joshua 11), having been so commanded by Moses...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Sichat Malakhei HaSharet 3:16 (§4): “And therefore the Sages taught (Berakhot 18b): the wicked in their lifetimes are called dead, for genuine life issues from the soul; but if one cleaves to corporeal lusts of the body, his soul-faculties remain mere shadows, and he is termed dead, just as upon the departure of his soul he is physically dead. But one who cleaves to Hashem God of Truth—which our Sages expounded (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 1:1; Bereishit Rabbah 81:2; Vayikra Rabbah 26:1): why is He called Truth? Because He is the living God and eternal King.” Connection to this note: In Sichat Malakhei HaSharet 3:16 (§4), Rav Tzadok develops this theme alongside Bereshit Rabbah 81, illuminating how the teaching in Divrei Chalomot 22 unfolds within Kisvei Rav Tzadok.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 19a: ‘“Those who pass through [overei],” these are people who transgress [overin] the will of the Holy One, Blessed be He. “Valley [emek]” indicates that their punishment is that Gehenna is deepened [ma’amikin] for them. “Of weeping [bakha]” and “turn it into a water spring [ma’ayan yeshituhu],” indicates that they weep [bokhin] and make tears flow like a spring [ma’ayan] of the foundations [shitin], meaning like a spring that descends to the foundations of the earth. “Moreover, the early rain covers it with blessings,” indicates that they accept the justice of God’s judgment, and say before Him: Master of the Universe, You have judged properly, You have acquitted properly, You have condemned…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 22, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Eruvin 19a) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“all descending regarding the miracle (Eruvin 19a), the base man dominating holy man temporarily to his own ruin, forced ultimately to regurgitate his prey; enthroning a king who concentrates that realm's shells] and...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Nazir 23b: ‘§ The Gemara returns to analyze in greater detail the above matter itself. Rav Yehuda said that Rav said: A person should always occupy himself with Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, as through these acts performed not for their own sake, good deeds for their own sake come about. The proof for this is that in reward for the forty-two offerings that the wicked Balak sacrificed (see Numbers, chapter 23), although he did not do so for the sake of Heaven but to facilitate the cursing of the Jewish people, nevertheless he merited that Ruth descended from him. Not only was he the forebear of a righteous convert, but also of King David. And this is as Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 22, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Nazir 23b) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“[this is the defilement of the covenant of the tongue, corresponding to the covenant of the flesh; and his downfall in Sisera through Yael, as “at her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay” (Judges 5:27), as our Sages of...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

[God] replied " Tomorrow you'll see how smart he is." When He created man what did God do? He brought all animals before the angels and asked them the names of all the animals and they did not know. God said to them "Do you want to know the wisdom of Man? paragraphs.text: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 1:22–23: “And as taught in the Gemara (Shabbat 88b), that the entire world was filled with sweet fragrances—which signifies that the universe was sweetened and refined through the sublime light of His absolute unity. And that is why the Gemara there raises the difficulty: Where did the second commandment go [if the fragrance of the first filled all space]? And it answers: The Holy One, blessed be He, brought forth a wind and cleared away each preceding fragrance—meaning that the infinite light was slightly concealed so that room remained to receive the second commandment.” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 1:22–23 clarifies the inner dimension of Shabbat 88b and directly illuminates Rav Tzadok's point in Divrei Chalomot 23.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Tiferet Yosef, Ki Tavo 2: “In the holy Zohar (Yitro 82b), the 613 mitzvot are called the ‘613 counsels of the Torah’ (taryag ittin de-oraita). paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 35b: ‘The Gemara interjects: What is the meaning when the verse states this? If this question is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yosei, this transgression was singled out to teach that one who lights a fire on Shabbat violates an ordinary prohibition, as opposed to the performance of other types of labor on Shabbat, for which one is liable to receive court-imposed capital punishment. If this question is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Natan, this transgression was singled out to divide the various labors and to establish liability to receive court-imposed capital punishment for performance of any one of them. The Gemara explains: As it is taught in a baraita: Kindling of fire…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 23, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Sanhedrin 35b) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“and in Sanhedrin 35b: "the heart of each man is his own," representing Lower Wisdom, the wisdom of Solomon, the Oral Torah surging from the hearts of Israel's sages, wherefore a sage is superior to a prophet (Bava...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Bava Batra 12a: ‘Rabba bar bar Ḥana says that Rabbi Yoḥanan says: With regard to alleyways that are open to another city, and through which one would ordinarily travel to reach that other city, if the residents of the city in which the alleyways are located wished to block them off, the residents of the city into which the alleyways open can prevent them from doing so, because they have a right to reach their city via those routes. The Gemara explains: It is not necessary to state that they can prevent them from blocking the alleyways when there is no alternative route to reach their town, but they can prevent them from blocking the alleyways even when there is an alternative route.’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 23, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Bava Batra 12a) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“wherefore a sage is superior to a prophet (Bava Batra 12a on "we will acquire a heart of wisdom"), heartfelt perception surpassing visionary prophecy; and of the heart's wisdom: "and my heart saw much wisdom," inner...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Exodus 30:12:1-34:35:1: ‘AND THOU SHALT GIVE IT FOR THE SERVICE OF THE APPOINTED TENT — From this statement you may learn that he (Moses) was commanded to take their census when they began to contribute towards the building of the Tabernacle, after the incident of the golden calf, because the pestilence had befallen them, as it is said, (Exodus 32:35) “and the Lord plagued the people”. A parable: To what may this be compared? To a flock that is dear to its owner upon which there fell pestilence. As soon as it ceased he said to the shepherd, “I beg of you, count my sheep and ascertain how many of them are left”. He did this to show that it (the flock) was dear to him (Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tisa 9). — It is,…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 23, Rav Tzadok cites this commentary and halakhic-kabbalistic exposition (Rashi on Exodus 30:12:1-34:35:1) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“Rashi (Ki Tisa) explaining that Da'at is the Holy Spirit, which is the prophecy of the Sages; Ramban noting that a scholar intuitively hitting upon the truth receives the Holy Spirit flowing from Supernal Wisdom, the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Bereshit 8: “Now the serpent was more subtle than any beast of the field. From this it appears that in the wild beasts of the field is found more wisdom than in domestic animals, for a domestic beast agrees in its mindset to be subjugated and disciplined under the hand of man, with man providing sustenance for its soul, and does not care to sustain its needs directly from Hashem's hand; whereas in the wild beast is found greater wisdom, in that it does not wish to receive its bounty through flesh and blood, and consents to live with measured austerity, provided that its sustenance be directly from Hashem, blessed be He, so that it gazes at all times unto the Giver.” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Bereshit 8 clarifies the inner dimension of Niddah 61a and directly illuminates Rav Tzadok's point in Divrei Chalomot 25.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 42:8: ‘“The refugee came and told Abram the Hebrew, and he was dwelling in the plains of Mamre the Emorite, brother of Eshkol and brother of Aner, and they were allies of Abram” (Genesis 14:13). “The refugee came” – Reish Lakish in the name of bar Kappara: This is Og; he is the “refugee.” Why is he called Og? Because he came and found Abram sitting and engaging in the mitzva of baking [unleavened] loaves [ugot] [for Passover]. His intentions [in informing Abraham] were not to act for the sake of Heaven. Rather, he said: ‘This Abraham is a zealot. If I say to him now: Your nephew has been taken captive, he will go out to war and be killed, and I will take his wife Sarai.’ The Holy One blessed be…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 25, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 42:8) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“scheming that Abraham fall in battle so he might take Sarah, viewing himself as Abraham's peer since having survived the Deluge, Og presumed himself free of fatal guilt, wherefore even Moses later feared his merit;...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Resisei Layla 16:1 (§5): “However, a sage clings to the supernal wisdom of Hashem, blessed be He, which abides within thought in the brain; there it is possible for two opposites to coexist within a single subject. paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 17: ‘“The Lord God formed from the ground every beast of the field and every bird of the heavens, and brought them to the man to see what he would call it; and whatever the man would call every living creature, that was its name” (Genesis 2:19). “The Lord God formed from the ground [every beast of the field]” – they raised a question before Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakai: It is written: “God said: Let the earth produce living creatures after their kinds” (Genesis 1:24). Why then does the verse state [here again]: “The Lord God formed [vayitzer] from the ground every beast of the field”? He said to them: There [the previous verse] it was referring to the creation [of the animals], and here it refers…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 25, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 17) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“rooted in Supernal Wisdom (Chochmah Elyonah) which Moses brought down, descending to Lower Wisdom (Malkhut, Oral Torah), whose lower feet can descend toward alien philosophy that opposes holy wisdom; breeding heresy...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 35a: ‘The Gemara answers: Rava interprets it in accordance with the statement that Rabbi Elazar says that Rabbi Yitzḥak says, as Rabbi Elazar says that Rabbi Yitzḥak says: Every fast day on which the distribution of charity [tzedaka] is left overnight, this is considered as if one spilled the blood of the poor people, as they fasted all day in the expectation that they would receive charity before the day was over in order to purchase food with which to break their fasts. As it is stated: “She that was full of justice [tzedek], righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers.” The Gemara clarifies: And this statement applies with regard to the delaying of the distribution of bread and dates,…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 25, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Sanhedrin 35a) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“the Oral Torah surging from the heart (aliba de-Rabbi Peloni; Sanhedrin 35a), the wisdom of the Sanhedrin welling from pure hearts anchored in Hashem, the Rock of their heart; opposite which lies the corrupted heart...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Resisei Layla 12:1 (§9): “In that lofty sphere, even one whose Torah was merely 'from the lip outward' is not utterly cast out, for that realm transcends the heart, and 'the end of action is bound up in the initial thought' in this physical world, which constitutes the World of Action; and the physical movement of one's lips is halakhically deemed an action, so that even within this outward speech holiness abides and serves to draw holiness inward into the heart through that mechanism.” Connection to this note: In Resisei Layla 12:1 (§9), Rav Tzadok develops this theme alongside Sanhedrin 35a, illuminating how the teaching in Divrei Chalomot 25 unfolds within Kisvei Rav Tzadok.

The Gemara offers a proof, as it is stated: “The fool said in his heart: ‘There is no God’; they have been corrupt, they have acted abominably; there is none who does good” (Psalms 14:1). paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 7a: ‘§ And the various Sages who offered interpretations of the verse: “And the covetous blesses himself, though he despises the Lord” (Psalms 10:3), disagree with the explanation of Rabbi Tanḥum bar Ḥanilai. paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:135 (§4): “And our Sages stated in Sotah (42b) that Goliath was the offspring of a hundred fathers and one dog (nanei), see Tosafot there; as I heard regarding the "hundred judgments" (Sanhedrin 7a), that when an attribute is in the heart it numbers ten, but in the brain each of the ten expands tenfold to become one hundred, and strife impacts the brain; and I heard concerning the dictum (Chagigah 9b), "One who reviews his lesson one hundred times is not comparable to one who reviews it one hundred and one times," for that additional "one" represents renewing from the transcendent source.” Connection to this note: In Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:135 (§4), Rav Tzadok develops this theme alongside Sanhedrin 7a, illuminating how the teaching in Divrei Chalomot 25 unfolds within Kisvei Rav Tzadok.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 10: ‘Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, Rabbi Yehuda says: Repentance accomplishes half and prayer accomplishes it all. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: Repentance accomplishes it all and prayer accomplishes half. According to Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi, repentance accomplishes half. From whom do you derive it? It is from Cain. An edict was decreed against him. Once he repented, half of the edict was withheld from him. From where is it derived that he repented? As it is stated: “Cain said to the Lord: My iniquity is too great to bear” (Genesis 4:13). From where is it derived that half the edict was withheld from him? That is what is written: “Cain departed from the presence of the Lord, and…’ Context and connection to Divrei Chalomot: In Divrei Chalomot 25, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Vayikra Rabbah 10) to illuminate his dream-vision and Torah exposition here (“out of supreme love for Israel resolving: "Better the disgrace be pinned upon me" (Vayikra Rabbah 10); through which he merited the high priesthood, consecrated as holy of holies. And this is Levi's sanctity: "Who...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on nocturnal Torah insights, the elevation of the soul's faculties during sleep, and the inner secrets of the Oral Torah developed in Divrei Chalomot.
